newsitem.title: USA: Penn. Turnpike short on funds for infrastructure.
newsitem.headline: Penn. Turnpike short on funds for infrastructure.

text.p: Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission is about $1.5 billion short in funds for a proposed major toll road project in southwest Pennsylvania that state legislators said is vital to keep the region out of economic peril.

According to a recently released report by the state's Legislative Budget and Finance Committee, the Commission's debt has ballooned in the last decade, leaving it lacking in funds for new infrastructure.
The project, called Mon-Fayette Expressway and Southern Beltway Transportation Project, has a projected total cost of $2.5 billion.
The new toll road system, first proposed in the mid 1980s, would link West Virginia, downtown Pittsburgh and the city's suburbs and international airport.

"I personally believe that we're never going to dig ourselves out of the economic decadence (in southwest Pennsylvania) of the 1980s and early 90s unless we build that road," said Rep. Frank Mascara, D-Charleroi.
Mascara said the current federal contribution to the project of $24 million isn't enough, and he is working with Congress to get $12 billion more in highway funds into the federal budget.

In 1985, when many of the region's steel mills were shutting down and the Commission was cash rich, the state General Assembly passed Act 61, giving the Commission the responsibility for building a series of mini-pikes to increase infrastructure.
According to the Budget and Finance Committee's report, the new construction ballooned the Commission's debt, from $65 million in 1986 to $1.2 billion last year.
Of every dollar in tolls it collects, 28 cents goes to debt service. In spite of the borrowing, the Commission is $1.5 billion short in funds for the proposed toll road system.

The money it does have, including the $28 million a year it will get from the 3.5 cent per gallon increase in the gas tax passed in April, will fund some sections of the project, but other sections are completely unfunded, according to the report.
"The financial and resource demands posed by Act 61 implementations appear to threaten the Turnpike's ability (to fund the project)," the report said.
Legislators and real estate officials said without the project, the region's economy will suffer because new business will be attracted to other cities that have better infrastructure.

"In Columbus, Ohio, employers can hire from their whole region because they have a sensible transportation system," said Pittsburgh realtor Ron Tarquinio. "If we don't get real on our roads...we're going to perish as a region. We need to build (this project) or we're going to perish."
